title: Lazy lists
scopeHtml: LazyColumn/LazyRow/LazyGrid internals, keys and contentType, item state, nested scrolling, sticky headers, scroll-driven UI, Paging 3 with Compose, performance traps and the RecyclerView comparison.

questions.promptHtml: When would you use LazyColumn and when is Column(Modifier.verticalScroll(...)) the right choice?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you understand that laziness is a cost trade-off, not a free upgrade.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Column composes, measures and lays out every child up front, even the ones off screen. LazyColumn only composes what is visible plus a small prefetch window, so cost scales with the viewport, not with the data size. For a small, bounded list, roughly a dozen items such as a settings form, Column plus verticalScroll is simpler and cheaper because there's no subcomposition or prefetch machinery. For anything unbounded or large, or with images, I use LazyColumn."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Column is a normal layout: all children are composed in the same composition pass, so N items means N compositions, N measures and N slot-table groups, regardless of scroll position. verticalScroll only gives the content infinite max height and translates it; nothing is skipped.

LazyColumn uses a LazyLayout which composes items on demand during the measure phase via subcomposition. Items that leave the viewport are disposed (or kept in a reuse pool); new ones are composed as they enter.

Column + verticalScroll (10,000 items)     LazyColumn (10,000 items)
composed:  10,000                          composed:  ~8 visible + prefetch
measured:  10,000                          measured:  ~8 visible + prefetch
memory:    O(N)                            memory:    O(viewport)

Costs of lazy: no intrinsic sizing across all items, scroll position math is estimated, item content is composed in a subcomposition (each item is its own composition root), and you can't read the total content size. The official performance guidance explicitly says to use plain Row/Column for small, bounded collections (about 1 to 10 items) to avoid lazy virtualization and prefetch overhead.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Fine: 6 fixed sections, needs intrinsic height behaviour, no recycling benefit
Column(Modifier.verticalScroll(rememberScrollState())) {
    sections.forEach { SettingsSection(it) }
}

// Required: unbounded feed
LazyColumn { items(feed, key = { it.id }) { FeedCard(it) } }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using Column + verticalScroll for a list loaded from network/DB: 2,000 rows compose in one frame, a multi-hundred-ms jank spike and an OOM risk with images.
  • Wrapping everything in LazyColumn "for performance", then fighting fillMaxHeight, sticky layout and intrinsics for a 5-item screen.
  • Putting a LazyColumn inside a verticalScroll Column (crash, see the nested scrolling question).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can't LazyColumn use IntrinsicSize? → Intrinsics need to measure all children; lazy layouts don't have all of them composed.
  2. Mixed screen: header form plus long list? → One LazyColumn with item {} blocks for the form and items for the list.
  3. How does a Column handle 200 light text rows? → Fine; the crossover is workload-dependent, so measure rather than guess.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "Lazy is like RecyclerView, use it for long lists." Senior states the cost model (compose work is O(N) vs O(viewport)), the overhead for small lists, and the intrinsic and measurement limits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A settings screen rebuilt as LazyColumn broke a Modifier.weight-based footer and shipped a regression; the fix was reverting to Column since the list was 8 items.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how the LazyColumn { } content block works. Why can't you call composables directly inside it, and what do item, items and itemsIndexed do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Common mistake source; reveals whether you know the lambda is a DSL builder, not composition.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The trailing lambda of LazyColumn is a LazyListScope.() -> Unit, a non-composable builder. It doesn't emit UI; it registers item definitions (count, key, contentType, and a composable content lambda per item). The lazy layout later calls those composable content lambdas only for visible indices. So composables go inside item { }/items { } lambdas, never directly in the builder body."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The block runs to produce an interval-based item provider: each item/items call adds an interval (startIndex, count, key fn, contentType fn, itemContent). The provider maps index to key and content. Because the builder isn't @Composable, you can't call Text() in it (compile error), and any plain code there (like list.sortedBy{}) runs whenever the provider is rebuilt, not per item.

LazyColumn { ... }        -> builds LazyListIntervalContent
   item { A }             -> interval [0,1)
   items(list) { B(it) }  -> interval [1, 1+n)
Measure pass: need index 3 -> find interval -> compose B(list[2]) in subcomposition

The builder lambda is re-executed when something it captures changes (it is held via an updated-state wrapper), producing a new provider. That is why heavy work in the builder body is a trap: it reruns on every relevant state change.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
LazyColumn {
    item { Header() }                                   // single
    items(users, key = { it.id }) { UserRow(it) }        // list
    itemsIndexed(users) { index, u -> RankedRow(index, u) } // when you need the index
    // Text("hi")  // compile error: not composable scope
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling users.indexOf(u) inside items instead of itemsIndexed; that is O(N) per item, O(N^2) overall (called out in the official perf guidance).
  • Doing sortedBy/filter in the builder body; do it in the ViewModel or remember.
  • Forgetting there are Array/List overloads, and that items(count) exists for index-only items.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is it LazyListScope not @Composable? → Items need to be addressable by index without composing them.
  2. Can I use forEach { item { } }? → Yes, but you lose interval compactness and per-item key arguments; prefer items.
  3. What re-runs when state read in the builder changes? → The builder, producing a new provider; visible items then recompose as needed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "items is like adapter." Senior: describes the interval-based provider and why builder-body work and indexOf hurt.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A screen sorted a 5k list inside the builder; every scroll-state read in the same scope re-sorted it, spiking CPU on mid-range devices.

questions.promptHtml: What is the key parameter in items(), what is the default, and why does it matter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Keys affect correctness (state), not just speed; a classic filter for real Compose experience.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The key is the item's identity. By default it's the item's position, so if the list reorders or an item is inserted or removed, Compose thinks 'item 3' is still the same item and gives it the old item 3's state. A stable unique key, like a database id, lets Compose track items across moves: it keeps remembered and rememberSaveable state with the right item, skips recomposition for moved items whose data didn't change, and enables animateItem."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Lazy layouts keep per-key records: the composition slot, rememberSaveable state (via a SaveableStateHolder keyed by the key), and scroll anchoring. Scroll position is also key-aware: when the data set changes, LazyListState uses the key of the first visible item to find where it moved, so the viewport stays on the same content instead of the same index.

Requirements per the official docs: keys must be unique, and must be saveable in a Bundle (primitives, String, Parcelable/Serializable), since they feed the saveable registry. Never use the index or hashCode().

Before: [A, B, C]  keys by index 0,1,2     Insert X at top
After:  [X, A, B, C] index keys 0..3  => slot0 (was A's state) now shows X. Wrong state, 3 extra recompositions
        id keys: A,B,C keep their slots, only X is composed

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
LazyColumn {
    items(items = notes, key = { it.id }) { note -> NoteRow(note) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Non-unique keys cause a crash: IllegalArgumentException: Key "..." was already used. If you are using LazyColumn/Row please make sure you provide a unique key for each item.
  • Using a non-Bundle-saveable key (a custom data class) crashes when state is saved.
  • Keying by something mutable such as a name or timestamp.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What about item { }? → It takes a key too; header items need stable keys for animations.
  2. Does a key help when only item contents change? → No; it only handles moves, inserts and removes. Content change needs a new data object and stable params.
  3. Key and scroll position? → State keeps the viewport anchored to the same key when data above changes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "keys improve performance." Senior: "keys define identity, so they fix state bugs, scroll anchoring and animation, and perf is a side effect."

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A todo app's checkboxes "moved" to other tasks after sorting by due date because rows used index keys and held local remember state.

questions.promptHtml: What does contentType do in lazy lists and when does omitting it hurt?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests knowledge of the reuse pool, which is Compose's partial answer to view recycling.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "When an item scrolls out, its composition and nodes can be kept in a reuse pool. contentType tells the lazy layout which items are structurally the same, so a slot is only reused for an item of the same type. Without it, all items share one type, so a 'photo card' slot may get reused for a 'text row', and the reuse has to rebuild most of the tree anyway, losing the benefit. In heterogeneous feeds I always set it."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Lazy layouts keep a small pool of unused item compositions. When a new index is needed, the layout asks the pool for a slot with the same content type (default null, meaning all items are one type), then re-composes it with the new data via a reusable-content mechanism. For same-shaped items, most groups in the slot table match, so recomposition mostly updates parameters and skips structure creation. Across different shapes, the recomposer must tear down and create nodes, which costs about as much as a fresh composition.

Pool: [Photo slot][Photo slot][Text slot]
Need index 40 (Photo): contentType=Photo -> reuse Photo slot (cheap)
                       contentType=null  -> may grab Text slot (expensive)

State note: reuse resets remember state inside the item, as the reused slot is treated as a new item identity-wise. Do not depend on remembered state surviving type reuse.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
LazyColumn {
    items(
        items = feed,
        key = { it.id },
        contentType = { item ->
            when (item) { is Post.Photo -> 0; is Post.Text -> 1; is Post.Ad -> 2 }
        }
    ) { FeedItem(it) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a too-granular type (e.g. the id) so nothing is reused.
  • Assuming it applies to item {} blocks without passing contentType there.
  • Expecting RecyclerView-style pooled ViewHolders with no re-composition; reuse still recomposes, it only skips structural work.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does it affect prefetch? → Prefetch composes into a slot of the appropriate type, so mismatches waste the prefetch.
  2. Cost when types are all identical? → Nothing; keep it unset or constant.
  3. Verify the benefit? → Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric on a scroll with and without it; compare P90/P99 frame duration.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average has never heard of it. Senior links it to the pool, explains why mismatched types waste reuse, and measures it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Mixed feed (image, video, ad cards) dropped P95 frame time after adding contentType; the improvement should be confirmed with a benchmark, since gains vary by item shape.

questions.promptHtml: How does LazyColumn work under the hood? Where does composition of items happen?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who use lazy lists from those who can debug them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "LazyColumn is built on LazyLayout, which uses SubcomposeLayout. During the measure pass it figures out which indices fit in the viewport using item provider data, and for each it subcomposes that item's content. So composition of items happens inside the layout phase, not during the parent's composition. After measure, items are placed; items that scroll off are disposed or pooled. A prefetch scheduler composes and measures upcoming items on idle time between frames."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Pieces:

  1. Item provider: built from your LazyListScope block (index to key, contentType, content).
  2. LazyListState: holds first visible index/offset, layoutInfo, and the scroll position as snapshot state.
  3. SubcomposeLayout: lets the layout call subcompose(slotId, content) during measure, creating child compositions on demand under the parent composition context (so CompositionLocals flow down).
  4. Measure result is a LazyListMeasureResult list of visible LazyListMeasuredItems.

Scroll flow: a drag updates the scroll offset in LazyListState (a snapshot-state write consumed in the layout phase) so a scroll remeasures without recomposing the parent. Only newly visible items compose. This is why scrolling a list doesn't recompose LazyColumn's caller.

state.scrollBy(dy) -> invalidate layout (not composition)
 measure: compute first visible index/offset
   for each needed index: subcompose(key, content[i])   <- composition happens here
 place items; dispose items beyond cache window
 idle: prefetch next item(s)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Reading list state in the *layout* phase avoids parent recomposition
Box(Modifier.offset { IntOffset(0, -state.firstVisibleItemScrollOffset) })

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reading state.firstVisibleItemIndex directly in composition: it recomposes the caller on every index change.
  • Assuming an item's remember survives scrolling away; the composition is disposed (or reset when reused).
  • Expecting LaunchedEffect inside an item to run only once; it restarts each time the item enters composition.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why are CompositionLocals available in items? → Subcomposition links to the parent composition context.
  2. Does scrolling trigger recomposition of the LazyColumn's parent? → No, only layout, unless you read state in composition.
  3. What does layoutInfo give you? → Visible item infos (index, key, offset, size), viewport size, total count; read via derivedStateOf/snapshotFlow.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it only renders visible items." Senior: SubcomposeLayout, measure-time composition, item provider, state read in layout phase.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Overscroll effects reading firstVisibleItemScrollOffset in composition recomposed the screen every frame until moved into a graphicsLayer lambda.

questions.promptHtml: What is prefetching in lazy lists, and how can you tune it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Perf-aware seniors know jank in flings comes from composition on the critical path.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Prefetch composes and measures upcoming items ahead of time, off the critical frame path, during idle time after a frame, so when they scroll into view the work is done. Historically it was about one item ahead in the scroll direction; in newer foundation versions the default is a LazyLayoutCacheWindow that prefetches a distance clamped between 10% and 50% of the viewport. For very tall items or very fast flings I can configure a larger ahead window, at the cost of memory and wasted work."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Without prefetch, a new item's composition, measure and first draw all occur inside the frame it appears, so a heavy item blows the 16.6 ms (60 Hz) or 8.3 ms (120 Hz) budget. With prefetch, the scheduler uses idle time to precompose and premeasure. In newer versions, prefetch composition can be paused/resumed across frames (verify the exact foundation version; the docs I read describe this under the cache window section, with API changes in Compose 1.13).

Per the official lists doc: all lazy collections use CacheWindow as the default strategy; ahead distance is clamped to 10%-50% of viewport. Small items (under about 10% of the viewport) get several items prefetched; items larger than 50% of the viewport are not fully covered, so late prefetch is possible and the docs advise raising aheadFraction.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// API as documented for Compose 1.13+ (verify against your version)
LazyColumn(
    cacheWindow = LazyLayoutCacheWindow(aheadFraction = 0.5f, behindFraction = 0.2f)
) { /* items */ }

Older versions took the strategy via rememberLazyListState(prefetchStrategy = ...) / cacheWindow on the state; the docs mark those as migrated.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Cranking aheadFraction to 2.0 "to be safe": memory grows and prefetch work competes with the main thread for image decoding.
  • Blaming prefetch when the real cost is a Coil decode on the main thread or a heavy remember {}.
  • Believing prefetch helps programmatic jumps; scrollToItem of a far index composes synchronously.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Nested lists? → Inner LazyRow items can be prefetched when the outer item is prefetched (nested prefetch, added to the foundation library; details version dependent).
  2. How would you prove it helps? → Macrobenchmark with FrameTimingMetric and StartupMode.WARM, CompilationMode.Partial baseline profile.
  3. Does it help in debug builds? → Debug builds are slow regardless; always benchmark release with R8 and a baseline profile.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it preloads the next item." Senior: idle-time scheduling vs frame budget, window clamping, memory trade-off, benchmarking.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A media feed with full-bleed 90%-viewport cards janked on flings until the ahead window was widened and measured.

questions.promptHtml: What happens to remember and rememberSaveable state inside lazy list items as they scroll out and back in?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Direct source of "my text field/expanded state resets" bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "When an item scrolls out of the composition window its composition is disposed, so remember state is lost. rememberSaveable inside items survives because lazy layouts wrap each item in a saveable state holder keyed by the item key: values are saved as it leaves and restored when it comes back. That requires the key to be Bundle-saveable and stable. Anything that must outlive that belongs in hoisted state, like the ViewModel."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each item composes inside SaveableStateProvider(key). On disposal, the registry calls the savers of the rememberSaveable entries and stores the result by key; on re-entry with the same key they restore. This storage is also part of the activity's saved instance state, so it can survive configuration change and process death, subject to Bundle size limits (~1 MB transaction limit shared across the whole process state).

Consequences:

  • Index keys: state goes to whichever item sits at that index later.
  • remember { mutableStateOf(expanded) } collapses on scroll. Fine for transient animations, wrong for user data.
  • With contentType reuse, remember also resets as the slot gets new content.
  • Sources of truth: for list-of-N item state (selection, expansion), hoist as Set<Id> in the ViewModel, so it survives and drives other UI (a selection toolbar).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
items(rows, key = { it.id }) { row ->
    var expanded by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(false) } // restored per key
    RowItem(row, expanded) { expanded = !expanded }
}
// Better when other UI needs it:
val expandedIds: Set<Long> by vm.expanded.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saving big objects with rememberSaveable in 1,000 items: saved-state bloat, TransactionTooLargeException risk.
  • Custom class as key without Parcelable.
  • Storing selection in per-item remember and wondering why "select all" can't work.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does rememberSaveable survive when the item is removed from data? → Entry is dropped with the key.
  2. State inside a LazyRow nested in a LazyColumn item? → Lives inside the outer item's saveable scope; the inner LazyListState is rememberSaveable so scroll position is restored if the outer key is stable.
  3. How does this interact with Paging placeholders? → Key comes from the data; null placeholders need a key fallback (see the Paging questions).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average knows "rememberSaveable survives scrolling." Senior explains the keyed saveable holder, key requirements, size limits, and hoists shared state.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Message-reply drafts typed in item text fields vanished on scroll until they moved to a ViewModel-backed map keyed by message id.

questions.promptHtml: How do you make sure list items skip recomposition when the list changes? Talk about parameters and stability.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Item recomposition is the main perf lever in lists and depends on stability rules plus compiler version.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A row skips when all its parameters are equal to last time (stable types compared with equals, unstable ones by instance under strong skipping). So I pass the individual immutable model to each row, keyed by id, and a lambda that doesn't capture changing state. With strong skipping, which is on by default in the Kotlin 2.0.20+ compiler plugin, unstable params compare by reference and lambdas are auto-remembered, but a fresh List or a new data instance with unchanged contents still defeats skipping unless equals says equal."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Without strong skipping (older compiler), any unstable parameter, notably List<T>, Set, classes from other modules with no stability config, forced the row to recompose whenever its parent did. Fix: @Immutable/@Stable, kotlinx ImmutableList, or a compiler stability config file.

With strong skipping (default from the Kotlin 2.0.20 compiler plugin; earlier opt-in via compiler flag since 1.5.4, verify per release): composables with unstable params can skip, using instance equality (===) for unstable ones and equals for stable ones. Lambdas capturing unstable values are remembered with those values as keys.

Row-level pattern:

parent recomposes (list changed)
 items(list, key=id) { row -> Row(row) }   // each Row param = one Message instance
 unchanged messages: same instance (or equals) -> skipped
 changed message: new instance -> only that row recomposes

The trap: mapping to new UI-model objects on every emission (list.map { it.toUi() } inside composition or a combine that recreates every object) produces new instances for unchanged data. With data class equality it's fine only if the type is stable (strong skipping uses === for unstable ones!).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Immutable
data class MessageUi(val id: Long, val text: String, val unread: Boolean)

LazyColumn {
    items(messages, key = { it.id }) { m ->
        MessageRow(m, onClick = { vm.open(m.id) }) // lambda capture of stable id
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Passing the whole UiState into each row.
  • List<Message> parameter on the row itself.
  • Assuming @Immutable is verified; it's a promise, a lie causes missed updates.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you check it? → Compose compiler reports (-reports/metrics destinations) show skippable and unstable params; Layout Inspector shows recomposition/skip counts.
  2. ImmutableList still needed with strong skipping? → Less often; still useful if you want equals-based comparisons.
  3. Stability of a type from another module? → Use the stability configuration file.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use @Immutable." Senior: strong skipping semantics, instance vs equals comparison, new-instance-per-emission mapping trap, and reads compiler reports.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A mapper recreating all UI models each emission made every visible row recompose on each poll; fixed with a diffing mapper preserving unchanged instances.

questions.promptHtml: How do stickyHeader, contentPadding and Modifier.animateItem() work, and what are their pitfalls?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Practical API fluency plus awareness of key-dependent behaviour.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "stickyHeader is a LazyListScope item that pins to the top of the viewport until the next header pushes it out. contentPadding pads the scrollable content area so items scroll under system bars or a FAB without clipping, unlike Modifier.padding on the list. animateItem animates placement (and optionally fade in/out) when items are reordered, inserted or removed, but it only works if each item has a stable key."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• stickyHeader: Sticky headers are laid out as normal items in the index space (so they count in itemCount and indices), but the layout re-places the current header at offset 0. It was historically marked @ExperimentalFoundationApi; check your foundation version for opt-in. Each header should have a key and contentType different from rows.
  • contentPadding: padding is inside the scrolling viewport; items clip at the list bounds, not at the padded edge. Essential with edge-to-edge. Modifier.padding would clip content at the padding edge.
  • animateItem: replaced the older animateItemPlacement (foundation 1.7, verify). Parameters: fadeInSpec, placementSpec, fadeOutSpec. It animates by tracking items by key; with index keys it animates the wrong things. Removal animation keeps the item in the layout temporarily during fade out.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
LazyColumn(contentPadding = PaddingValues(bottom = 88.dp)) { // room for FAB
    grouped.forEach { (day, msgs) ->
        stickyHeader(key = "h_$day", contentType = "header") { DayHeader(day) }
        items(msgs, key = { it.id }, contentType = { "msg" }) { m ->
            MessageRow(m, Modifier.animateItem())
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Header keys colliding with item keys, causing the duplicate-key crash.
  • Transparent sticky headers showing rows scrolling under them (give a background).
  • Using animateItem plus animateContentSize on same item causing stutter.
  • Forgetting animateItem must be applied to the item's root modifier chain.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to know which header is current? → derivedStateOf { state.layoutInfo.visibleItemsInfo } mapping to the header key.
  2. Index math with headers? → Headers are real indices; account for them in scrollToItem.
  3. Reorder drag-and-drop? → Needs a custom or library approach; animateItem handles placement of the rest.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists the APIs. Senior mentions key dependence, index space, clipping semantics of contentPadding vs padding, and key collisions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Chat date headers used "2024-05-01" as key and a message id happened to match a string key format in a debug fixture; crash only surfaced in QA data.

questions.promptHtml: You want a "scroll to top" button that appears after the user scrolls past the first item. How do you implement it without recomposing on every scroll pixel?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Canonical derivedStateOf use case; tests understanding of state reads and invalidation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "listState.firstVisibleItemIndex changes as the user scrolls, so reading it directly in composition recomposes that scope whenever the index changes. I wrap the boolean in remember { derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0 } } so the composable only recomposes when the boolean flips. For lightweight conditions on fast-changing state, the docs also describe computedStateOf in Compose Runtime 1.13+ (verify availability in your version)."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Composition tracks which State objects were read in a scope; a write to any invalidates it. firstVisibleItemIndex is itself backed by derived state, but it still changes each time a new item becomes first, and firstVisibleItemScrollOffset changes every pixel. derivedStateOf creates a state whose readers are invalidated only when the result changes (by equality), with the calculation re-run whenever its dependencies change.

Two rules from the official guidance: the dependencies read inside the lambda (such as listState.firstVisibleItemIndex) must not be passed as remember keys, since that recreates the derived state on every change and defeats it; and a trivially cheap derivation isn't always worth derivedStateOf overhead.

Better still for purely visual effects: don't recompose at all. Read the offset in layout/draw (Modifier.offset { }, graphicsLayer { }, drawBehind), as these lambda reads skip composition.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val listState = rememberLazyListState()
val showButton by remember { derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0 } }
Box {
    LazyColumn(state = listState) { /* ... */ }
    AnimatedVisibility(showButton, Modifier.align(Alignment.BottomEnd)) {
        FloatingActionButton(onClick = { scope.launch { listState.animateScrollToItem(0) } }) { Icon(Icons.Default.KeyboardArrowUp, null) }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• val showButton = listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0 in the same scope as the whole screen.
  • Using derivedStateOf for every boolean; if the input changes as rarely as the output, it's overhead.
  • Reading listState.layoutInfo in composition for sizes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. derivedStateOf vs snapshotFlow? → derivedStateOf feeds composition; snapshotFlow is for side effects/analytics on state changes.
  2. Hide toolbar based on scroll direction? → Track previous index/offset in snapshotFlow or NestedScrollConnection rather than composition.
  3. Why not remember(listState.firstVisibleItemIndex)? → Recreates the derived state each change; no dampening.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use derivedStateOf." Senior explains invalidation granularity, key misuse, and moves purely visual scroll effects to layout/draw reads.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A collapsing header read firstVisibleItemScrollOffset in composition and recomposed the whole screen at 120 fps; moving it into graphicsLayer {} dropped CPU noticeably.

questions.promptHtml: How do you control and observe scroll position programmatically? Compare scrollToItem, animateScrollToItem, and using snapshotFlow on the state.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Practical; also probes coroutine/scroll mutex semantics.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "LazyListState.scrollToItem(index, offset) jumps immediately, animateScrollToItem animates and is cancelable, both are suspend functions that need a coroutine, typically rememberCoroutineScope, and they take the scroll mutex so a user drag interrupts them. To observe, I use snapshotFlow { state.firstVisibleItemIndex } in a LaunchedEffect for analytics or pagination triggers, with distinctUntilChanged and optionally drop/filter."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• State is saved via rememberLazyListState() (it uses rememberSaveable), so scroll position survives configuration change.
  • Scrolling is MutatorMutex-protected: starting a new programmatic scroll cancels the previous; a user gesture takes priority (MutatePriority.UserInput).
  • animateScrollToItem to a far index doesn't animate across all items; it scrolls a bounded distance, then snaps, to keep it cheap. Exact behaviour is an implementation detail (verify).
  • layoutInfo exposes visibleItemsInfo, totalItemsCount, viewportSize; use for "load more when last visible >= total - 5".
  • canScrollForward/canScrollBackward are state properties.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val state = rememberLazyListState()
LaunchedEffect(state) {
    snapshotFlow { state.layoutInfo.visibleItemsInfo.lastOrNull()?.index }
        .filterNotNull().distinctUntilChanged()
        .collect { last -> if (last >= totalCount - 5) onLoadMore() }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling scrollToItem from composition body (side effect in composition).
  • Trigger "load more" via LaunchedEffect(state.firstVisibleItemIndex): restarts constantly; use snapshotFlow.
  • Forgetting that scrollToItem on an item index changes meaning when the dataset changes; key-aware anchoring only applies to data changes, not your stored index.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Restore position after process death? → rememberLazyListState is saveable; for ViewModel-driven restore, store index+offset and pass initialFirstVisibleItemIndex.
  2. Reverse layout "stick to bottom"? → Compare firstVisibleItemIndex == 0 before inserting; see the chat scenario later.
  3. Why does the animation stop on touch? → MutatorMutex priority.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: calls the APIs. Senior: mutex semantics, snapshotFlow for observation, saveable state, and the pagination trigger pitfalls.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An analytics "item impression" bug fired on every minor scroll because the effect was keyed on firstVisibleItemScrollOffset.

questions.promptHtml: How do you display a Paging 3 flow in a LazyColumn? What do collectAsLazyPagingItems, itemKey and itemCount give you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Paging is the standard for infinite lists; the Compose glue has traps (null placeholders, keys, load states).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The ViewModel exposes Flow<PagingData<T>> cached in viewModelScope with cachedIn. In Compose I call collectAsLazyPagingItems(), which returns a LazyPagingItems<T> with itemCount, indexer items[index] and loadState. I use items(count = lazyItems.itemCount, key = lazyItems.itemKey { it.id }, contentType = lazyItems.itemContentType { ... }). Indexing lazyItems[index] also triggers loading of nearby pages, and it may return null for placeholders."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
LazyPagingItems wraps a PagingDataDiffer. Accessing an index calls get(index), which reports an access hint to the Pager, which prefetches according to PagingConfig.prefetchDistance. Hence reading items is what triggers loads (the official sample does exactly this). itemKey returns a lambda mapping index to key, handling null placeholders by using a placeholder key (verify behavior for your paging-compose version). The docs I read show paging-compose at 3.5.3 in their setup snippet.

Loading UI: lazyItems.loadState.refresh/append/prepend are LoadState.Loading/NotLoading/Error. Show full-screen progress for refresh, footer item for append, error with retry().

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val items = vm.pager.collectAsLazyPagingItems()
LazyColumn {
    items(count = items.itemCount, key = items.itemKey { it.id }) { index ->
        items[index]?.let { MessageRow(it) } ?: Placeholder()
    }
    if (items.loadState.append is LoadState.Loading) item { CircularProgressIndicator() }
}
// ViewModel
val pager = Pager(PagingConfig(pageSize = 30)) { source }.flow.cachedIn(viewModelScope)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting cachedIn(viewModelScope): re-collection after rotation refetches or throws on collecting twice.
  • Not setting keys, so prepend/refresh jumps scroll.
  • Applying .filter/.map of PagingData in the composable instead of the ViewModel.
  • Using items.itemSnapshotList in composition for rendering instead of index access (stops prefetch triggers).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you handle refresh/pull-to-refresh? → items.refresh(), check loadState.refresh.
  2. Test? → paging-testing asSnapshot, TestPager.
  3. Offline? → RemoteMediator with Room as single source.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: wires it up. Senior knows access-triggers-load, placeholders/nulls, keys, cachedIn, and where transformations belong.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Missing cachedIn caused double network loads on every configuration change.

questions.promptHtml: Why can't you put a LazyColumn inside a vertically scrolling Column? What are the correct ways to build a screen with a header, a horizontal carousel and a long list?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Very frequent crash and design question; tests constraints model.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A verticalScroll container measures its child with infinite max height. A LazyColumn needs a finite viewport to know how many items to compose, so Compose throws IllegalStateException: Vertically scrollable component was measured with an infinite maximum height constraints. The fix is a single scroll container: one LazyColumn with item {} blocks for the header and the carousel (LazyRow inside an item is fine, because it scrolls on the other axis), then items {} for the list."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Constraints flow down. verticalScroll gives maxHeight = Infinity. A lazy list can't virtualize without a bounded viewport; if you "fix" it by Modifier.height(5000.dp) it composes... only what fits in 5000 dp, defeating the purpose, and breaks nested fling.

Correct structure:

LazyColumn
 ├ item { Header }
 ├ item { LazyRow { items(banners) } }    // cross-axis nesting is OK
 ├ stickyHeader { Tabs }
 └ items(feed) { FeedRow }

Same-axis nesting with bounded height (a LazyColumn with Modifier.height(300.dp) inside another LazyColumn) compiles and works but gives two competing scrolls: nested-scroll dispatches deltas inner first, then outer; flings are handled via NestedScrollConnection. Avoid for UX unless inner is a distinct panel.

For genuinely nested content you need all of (e.g. expand a short list inline): use a plain Column for the bounded few items, or compute forEach inside an item.

For a collapsing toolbar, use nestedScroll(connection) with Scaffold + TopAppBarDefaults.exitUntilCollapsedScrollBehavior().

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
LazyColumn {
    item { Header() }
    item { LazyRow(contentPadding = PaddingValues(horizontal = 16.dp)) { items(banners, key = { it.id }) { Banner(it) } } }
    items(feed, key = { it.id }) { FeedRow(it) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Giving a fixed height to dodge the crash and shipping a list that composes everything (or clips).
  • Applying fillMaxHeight in an item of a LazyColumn (unbounded) causing the same crash for a nested lazy.
  • Nested LazyVerticalGrid in LazyColumn: use LazyVerticalGrid with span for headers instead.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Grid with a header? → item(span = { GridItemSpan(maxLineSpan) }).
  2. Inner list should scroll first, then outer? → Default nested-scroll behaviour is inner first for drag; customise with NestedScrollConnection.
  3. Can the inner LazyRow state survive scrolling away? → rememberLazyListState inside the item is saved via the outer item's saveable scope if the outer key is stable.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "don't nest, use one LazyColumn." Senior: constraint mechanism, cross-axis OK, grid spans, nested-scroll connections, and the fake-height trap.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "temporary" heightIn(max = 4000.dp) workaround froze a screen with 800 categories; it was composing hundreds of rows.

questions.promptHtml: Compare LazyColumn and RecyclerView. What does each do better, and how do you decide for a new feature?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests balanced engineering judgement on migration and mixed codebases.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "RecyclerView recycles views: ViewHolders are bound and rebound, with DiffUtil for animations and mature features like item touch helper, snapping, and prefetch of the layout manager. LazyColumn disposes or reuses compositions, with state declared via keys, so no adapter/ViewHolder boilerplate and no diffing step (you update state and recomposition handles it). RecyclerView is still more predictable for extreme lists and has a mature ecosystem; LazyColumn wins on developer velocity and composability. For new screens in a Compose app I choose LazyColumn and fall back to AndroidView RecyclerView only for a proven gap."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Aspect RecyclerView LazyColumn
Unit of reuse ViewHolder (inflated views) Composition slot (by contentType)
Item identity getItemId/DiffUtil key
Updates Diff, then notify Recompose with new data
Item animations ItemAnimator animateItem
Prefetch GapWorker (RV prefetch) Idle-time precompose/premeasure
Heavy item cost Inflate (once) + bind Composition + measure per bind (cheaper reuse in same contentType)
Ecosystem Drag/swipe helpers, snap helpers, sticky libs Newer; drag-reorder via libraries or custom
State In views/ViewHolder In composition/saveable by key

Perf: both can hit 60/120 fps; Compose cost is higher without release build, R8 and baseline profiles (debug Compose lists are known to be much slower, so benchmark only release). RV needs less warmup. Benchmark yourself rather than quote numbers.

Decision factors: existing codebase, team skill, special features (item decoration, ConcatAdapter, ItemTouchHelper), data volume and item complexity, Paging (both supported).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Escape hatch only when justified
AndroidView(factory = { ctx -> RecyclerView(ctx).apply { layoutManager = LinearLayoutManager(ctx); adapter = myAdapter } })

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Judging Compose lists on a debug build.
  • Rewriting working RV screens purely for fashion.
  • Putting a RecyclerView inside AndroidView inside LazyColumn items (nested scroll mismatches).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does LazyColumn have view recycling? → Composition reuse by contentType, not view recycling.
  2. How would you migrate a screen incrementally? → See the migration scenario later.
  3. Item decorations equivalent? → Compose spacing via Arrangement.spacedBy, dividers as items; no decoration API.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Compose is newer and simpler." Senior: reuse unit, identity model, measured trade-offs, and a decision framework.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team measured P95 frame time after migrating a complex feed: improved after baseline profiles but only matched RV once images were pre-sized.

questions.promptHtml: A LazyColumn of rows, each containing a LazyRow carousel. What performance and state problems arise, and how do you handle them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Very common feed layout; reveals prefetch, state and memory understanding.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Each carousel is a full lazy layout with its own state, composition cache and prefetch. Problems: first appearance of a row composes the carousel's visible items synchronously (jank), scroll position of each LazyRow is lost if its state isn't saved per row, and memory grows with N rows times items. Mitigations: nested prefetch, stable keys on both levels, per-row rememberLazyListState under a stable outer key, contentType per carousel type, and modest item counts."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Compose foundation added prefetching for nested lazy lists: when the outer list prefetches a row, it can also prefetch a few inner items (nestedPrefetchItemCount; default 2 in the older LazyListPrefetchStrategy API, which is experimental/migrating to cache windows; verify for your version). Outer item composition cost = row chrome + inner list setup + first N inner items; without nested prefetch the inner items compose on the critical path.

State: rememberLazyListState() inside the outer item is saveable and keyed under the outer key, so scrolling away and back restores the carousel position. Using remember loses it, and index outer keys misassign it.

Outer item (key = section.id)
  rememberLazyListState()   -> saved by outer key
  LazyRow(state) items(inner, key = inner.id)

Memory: images in carousels; use size-aware image loading (Coil size), avoid decoding full-size bitmaps.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
items(sections, key = { it.id }, contentType = { "carousel" }) { section ->
    val rowState = rememberLazyListState()
    Column {
        SectionTitle(section.title)
        LazyRow(state = rowState, contentPadding = PaddingValues(horizontal = 16.dp)) {
            items(section.items, key = { it.id }) { Poster(it) }
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using section.items as a fresh list each emission (new instance) without skip-friendly models.
  • Same inner keys across different carousels aren't a problem (scoped), but duplicate within a carousel crash.
  • Setting the inner list fillMaxHeight().

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to verify nested prefetch helps? → Perfetto/System Trace with Compose tracing enabled to see when item composition runs (inside vs outside the frame), plus Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric on a warm scroll.
  2. Many carousels with sync scroll (like a sticky timeline)? → Share a ScrollState carefully; separate events.
  3. 10x data? → Keep inner windows bounded with Paging.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "put LazyRow in LazyColumn." Senior: separates state, prefetch, memory and key concerns and verifies with traces.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A home screen with 12 carousels lost scroll positions on back navigation until row state moved under stable section keys.

questions.promptHtml: Give me the list of things that most often make a LazyColumn slow in production, and how you'd find each one.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A senior should have a diagnostic checklist, not guesses.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I split it into three buckets. Work in the builder or composition: sorting, indexOf, allocations, collecting flows per item. Over-recomposition: missing keys, unstable params, state read too high. Per-item cost: heavy layouts, nested lazy lists, main-thread image decode, missing contentType. And first I rule out the measurement error: debug build, no R8, no baseline profile. I find each with release-build Macrobenchmark plus Layout Inspector recomposition counts and a system trace."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Checklist (several straight from the official best-practices page):

  1. items(list.sortedWith(...)) in composition: sort once with remember(list, cmp) or in the ViewModel.
  2. list.indexOf(item) in items: O(N^2). Use itemsIndexed.
  3. Missing key: moves recompose everything below.
  4. Missing contentType in heterogeneous lists.
  5. Reading state too high: pass lambdas (() -> Int) or use lambda modifiers (offset {}, graphicsLayer {}, drawBehind {}) so scroll-driven values skip composition.
  6. Collecting a shared Flow or reading LocalContext.current/LocalDensity.current per item instead of once above the list and passing values down.
  7. Backwards writes (writing state after reading it in the same composition) causing recomposition loops.
  8. Unstable params and new-instance mapping each emission.
  9. Item layouts with deep nesting, SubcomposeLayout-based widgets (BoxWithConstraints) per item.
  10. Large images decoded at full size.
  11. Debug-mode measurement.
Symptom -> Tool
dropped frames while flinging      -> Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric (release)
which composables recompose        -> Layout Inspector recomposition counts
why not skippable                  -> compiler reports (unstable params)
main thread blocking               -> Perfetto/system trace

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Bad
LazyColumn { items(contacts.sortedWith(cmp)) { ContactRow(it) } }
// Good
val sorted = remember(contacts, cmp) { contacts.sortedWith(cmp) }
LazyColumn { items(sorted, key = { it.id }) { ContactRow(it) } }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Optimising on a debug build.
  • Adding remember everywhere (comparing a large list key can cost more than the calculation, as the docs warn).
  • Adding derivedStateOf around cheap reads.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What's the quickest check that it's not your code? → Compare release with baseline profile on same device.
  2. How do you prevent regressions? → Macrobenchmark scroll test in CI with a threshold.
  3. Item has remember { } heavy init? → Move to ViewModel/precompute off main.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists "use keys." Senior has an ordered diagnostic method and verifies with tools.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: One team's "list jank" was 80% debug-build profiling; the real culprit was one indexOf in a 3k-item list.

questions.promptHtml: In a Paging 3 + Compose list, how do you handle refresh, append and prepend states, errors, placeholders, and keeping scroll position on refresh?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Paging UI edge cases are where production bugs live.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I read loadState.refresh for the full-screen states (initial loading, empty, error with retry), append for a footer item (spinner or an inline retry), and prepend similarly. With enablePlaceholders = true, items[index] can be null so I render a skeleton and give itemKey a stable fallback. On refresh, keys keep the viewport anchored to the same item when the new data still contains it; otherwise it resets to the top, which is usually the right behaviour after pull-to-refresh."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
CombinedLoadStates includes refresh/prepend/append plus source and mediator for RemoteMediator setups. Typical mapping:

refresh=Loading & itemCount==0      -> full screen progress
refresh=Error   & itemCount==0      -> full screen error + items.retry()
refresh=NotLoading & itemCount==0   -> empty state
append=Loading                      -> footer spinner item
append=Error                        -> footer "retry" item

Note: an Error on refresh with cached items (RemoteMediator) should show a snackbar, not a full-screen error.

Placeholders: PagingConfig(enablePlaceholders = true) requires PagingSource to supply itemsBefore/itemsAfter (count known). Items outside loaded pages are null. Without keys they animate/jump oddly.

Scroll on refresh: the Paging diff produces a new list; lazy anchoring uses keys. If you want "stay at top on refresh" explicitly, call listState.scrollToItem(0) after refresh completes via snapshotFlow on load state.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
LazyColumn(state = listState) {
    items(items.itemCount, key = items.itemKey { it.id }, contentType = items.itemContentType { "msg" }) { i ->
        items[i]?.let { MessageRow(it) } ?: SkeletonRow()
    }
    when (val s = items.loadState.append) {
        is LoadState.Loading -> item(key = "append_loading") { Spinner() }
        is LoadState.Error -> item(key = "append_error") { RetryRow(s.error) { items.retry() } }
        else -> Unit
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Footer items with no key (key collision with indexes from items; use string keys different from data keys, or ensure types differ).
  • Treating itemCount == 0 as empty while refresh is still loading.
  • Using refresh() vs retry() incorrectly: retry re-attempts failed loads, refresh reloads the whole dataset.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Duplicates from server across pages? → Keys collide and crash; dedupe in PagingSource or map keys.
  2. Showing a "new items" pill? → Compare with snapshotFlow on refresh completing.
  3. Offline-first? → RemoteMediator, Room as single source of truth, mediator load states.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: shows a spinner at the end. Senior has a full state table, handles empty/error with cache, and keys/placeholders.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An "empty state" flashed briefly on every open because it used itemCount == 0 without checking refresh state.

questions.contextHtml:
A task app (about 2M DAU) has a to-do list of up to 300 tasks. Each row has a checkbox with local state for an animation and an expand toggle. After "Delete" on row 3, QA reports that the expanded state moves to the row that was originally 4th, and sometimes the checkbox appears checked on another task. No crash. Code:

@Composable
fun TaskList(tasks: List<Task>, onDelete: (Long) -> Unit) {
    LazyColumn {
        items(tasks) { task ->
            var expanded by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(false) }
            TaskRow(task, expanded, { expanded = !expanded }, { onDelete(task.id) })
        }
    }
}

Red herring: the team suspects the ViewModel's StateFlow emits stale data. Logs show the emitted list is correct.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug and fix it. What else would you tighten?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the ViewModel or says "replace rememberSaveable with remember." That hides the symptom for scroll but doesn't fix identity, and it loses state on rotation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the state in the row or in the ViewModel? (row). Are task ids unique and stable? (Room rowid). Does it reproduce after sort order changes too? (yes, which implicates identity.) Any reuse of ids after deletes? (no).
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add key = { it.id }; a one-line hotfix we can ship.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) default key = index so item state tracks position; (b) ViewModel emits stale list (logs rule it out); (c) TaskRow internal state; (d) DiffUtil-like behaviour I might assume exists (it doesn't).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log task.id in the row's DisposableEffect to see which slot gets which id; reproduce in a UI test with composeTestRule deleting item 3 and asserting the expanded id; Layout Inspector to see row recomposition counts.
  5. Root cause: Without a key, a slot's identity is its index. rememberSaveable is stored per key, so after deleting index 2, index 3's old state is now delivered to the item now at index 3 (formerly 4th).
  6. Fix:
items(tasks, key = { it.id }) { task -> ... }

Long-term: hoist expandedIds: Set<Long> into the ViewModel if other UI depends on it, and add Modifier.animateItem() for delete animation. 7. Prevention: Lint/review checklist "every items has a key"; detekt rule or custom lint; UI test deleting/reordering with local state. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not switching to remember (loses rotation state); not using hashCode() as a key (collisions, not saveable guarantees).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Server can return the same id twice? → Crash Key ... was already used; dedupe in repository.
  • Key is a UUID object? → Not Bundle-saveable; use toString().
  • Why did it work in testing? → Lists were append-only in tests, so index = identity.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: a checklist feature shipped with index keys and passed QA because items were only appended; after launch, "sort by priority" shuffled expanded rows across tasks. The fix was one line, the test gap was the real lesson.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the data layer or replaces rememberSaveable with remember.
  • Hire: identifies index keys and adds key = { it.id }.
  • Strong hire: also explains per-key saveable storage, hoists shared state, adds animateItem and a regression UI test.

questions.contextHtml:
Release 5.12 of a shopping app (3M DAU) adds a "Recommended for you" section under the product details. Crash rate jumps from 0.2% to 1.9% within hours, all on the product screen. Stack excerpt:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: Vertically scrollable component was measured with an infinite maximum height constraints, which is disallowed.
 One of the common reasons is nesting layouts like LazyColumn and Column(Modifier.verticalScroll()).
 ...

The product screen is Column(Modifier.verticalScroll(rememberScrollState())) { Gallery(); Info(); Recommendations() } and Recommendations is a LazyColumn. It worked in the debug build for QA because the recommendations flag was off. Staged rollout is at 20%. Red herring: crash only on devices with large font scale, a mistake from a correlation in Crashlytics (flag cohort overlaps).
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through your response.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap the LazyColumn in a fixed height." That ships a degraded, lazy-less list and possible clipped content.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the flag server-side (can I kill it)? Yes. What's the rollout percentage and can I halt it? What's the recommendation list size (about 20)? Any other lazy layouts inside scroll containers? Is it only when recs non-empty?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Turn off the remote flag, halt the staged rollout, and roll back to 5.11 if flag kill doesn't cover it. Confirm the crash rate drops.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) lazy inside verticalScroll (the message says it); (b) large font scale (red herring: correlated with flag cohort); (c) a fillMaxHeight in an item. Check the stack points to LazyColumn measured in ScrollingLayoutNode.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce locally with the flag on; check Crashlytics breakdown by flag, not by font scale; a UI test that renders the screen with recs enabled.
  5. Root cause: verticalScroll measures children with infinite max height; LazyColumn needs a bounded viewport, so it throws.
  6. Fix: Short-term: for 20 recs, render a plain Column with forEach (bounded list; the official guidance says plain Column is fine for small bounded lists). Long-term: convert the whole screen to one LazyColumn with item {} blocks for Gallery and Info and items(recs) for the list so there's one scroll container.
LazyColumn {
    item { Gallery() }
    item { Info() }
    items(recs, key = { it.id }) { RecRow(it) }
}
  1. Prevention: Screenshot/UI tests with all flags on; a CI check running screens with flag permutations; the crash is deterministic so a test would have caught it; release checklist for flag-gated UI.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a fixed height (clips, composes everything, breaks fling); not userScrollEnabled=false on the inner (still infinite height crash).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Recs grow to 500? → Use the single LazyColumn plus Paging.
  • Need the header collapsing? → nestedScroll with TopAppBarScrollBehavior.
  • Why debug fine? → The code path never executed (flag).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: flag-gated UI shipped with only the flag-off path tested; 100% of flag-on users crashed. The post-incident action was a "all flags on" Compose UI smoke suite.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fixed-height hack; no rollback.
  • Hire: kills flag, rolls back, restructures to one lazy container or a Column for small lists.
  • Strong hire: dismisses the font-scale red herring with data, explains constraints, adds flag-permutation tests.

questions.contextHtml: A social feed (5M DAU, mix of 55% low-end Android Go-class devices) has P95 frame time 38 ms and 9% janky frames while scrolling, measured in the field via JankStats. Items: text post, image post, video post, ad. The list is LazyColumn { items(posts) { PostCard(it) } }, about 200 loaded items. Perfetto shows spikes of Compose:recompose on the main thread when a new item scrolls in (about 18 ms) and Coil decode on main for some images. Debug builds were used for the first investigation. Backend refresh every 30 s replaces the whole list.
questions.promptHtml: How do you reduce jank, and how do you prove it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add remember and derivedStateOf everywhere" with no measurement, no release-build testing.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 38 ms in release builds with R8 and a baseline profile? Which devices? Does jank correlate with item type? Are posts keyed? Are list updates every 30 s causing a re-render of everything?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ensure the release build ships a baseline profile and R8 (Compose without these is often much slower); cap image decode size.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) no keys and new instances each refresh: 30 s refresh recomposes 200 rows; (b) no contentType across 4 item types; (c) unstable params; (d) image decoding on main thread / full-size bitmaps; (e) tall items beyond default prefetch window.
  4. How I'd verify each: Macrobenchmark scroll with FrameTimingMetric on a low-end device in release; Layout Inspector recomposition counts after a refresh; compiler reports for unstable params; Perfetto on main thread, to see composition inside the frame vs idle prefetch.
  5. Root cause: Composition of newly visible items lands in the frame (heavy item plus unreused slot), and refresh churns identity so stable rows recompose.
  6. Fix: Short-term: key = { it.id }, contentType = { it.type }, diff-preserving mapper to keep unchanged instances, Coil size/precision to decode to display size. Long-term: lighter item layouts, widen cache window for tall cards (docs: default clamps 10%-50% of viewport), baseline profile including scroll interaction.
  7. Prevention: CI Macrobenchmark with P90/P99 thresholds, JankStats dashboards by device class.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not raising ahead window to huge (memory, low-end devices); not rewriting to RecyclerView before measuring.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Video items autoplay? → Players off the composition thread; play only the most visible via snapshotFlow.
  • Improvement of 38 to 22 ms isn't enough? → Check overdraw and layer usage, reduce nesting.
  • How do you attribute gains? → A/B each change on the same device/build with Macrobenchmark.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Composite: the first 30% win came from simply benchmarking release with a baseline profile; the rest from keys and a mapper preserving instances.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: random remember/derivedStateOf, debug measurements.
  • Hire: keys, contentType, release/baseline profile, measures with Macrobenchmark.
  • Strong hire: ties refresh churn to identity, handles image decode and cache window trade-offs, sets CI thresholds.

questions.contextHtml:
A news app has a long LazyColumn and a "Back to top" button plus a collapsing header title. Profiling on a mid-range phone (about 60 Hz) shows the whole ArticleScreen recomposing about 60 times per second while scrolling, with CPU at 35% on the main thread and occasional dropped frames. Code:

@Composable
fun ArticleScreen(articles: List<Article>) {
    val listState = rememberLazyListState()
    val showTop = listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0
    val titleAlpha = 1f - (listState.firstVisibleItemScrollOffset / 300f).coerceIn(0f, 1f)

    Box {
        LazyColumn(state = listState) { items(articles, key = { it.id }) { ArticleRow(it) } }
        Title(Modifier.alpha(titleAlpha))
        if (showTop) BackToTop()
    }
}

Red herring: someone blames ArticleRow for being slow; row counts in Layout Inspector are low.
questions.promptHtml: Why does this recompose so much, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap it in remember." remember doesn't help since the read is the problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the recomposing scope the screen or the rows? Do rows' counts stay flat (yes)? Is it release?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move the offset reads into lambdas so they stop invalidating the screen scope.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) firstVisibleItemScrollOffset read in composition changes every pixel, invalidating ArticleScreen; (b) firstVisibleItemIndex read in composition; (c) rows (ruled out: counts low).
  4. How I'd verify each: Layout Inspector recomposition counts for ArticleScreen rising with scroll; temporarily remove the alpha line and watch counts.
  5. Root cause: State read during composition makes that composition scope depend on the state. Each scroll delta writes the offset state and re-invokes ArticleScreen.
  6. Fix:
val showTop by remember { derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0 } }
Title(Modifier.graphicsLayer {
    alpha = 1f - (listState.firstVisibleItemScrollOffset / 300f).coerceIn(0f, 1f)
})
if (showTop) BackToTop()

graphicsLayer {} reads in the draw/layer phase, so no recomposition at all; derivedStateOf recomposes only when the boolean flips. (Note Modifier.alpha(value) takes a value so it reads in composition.) 7. Prevention: Review rule: "scroll state reads inside lambdas"; Layout Inspector check in PR for scroll screens. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not wrapping the offset in derivedStateOf (it still changes every pixel); the first-item-only offset also resets after the first item scrolls away, so for a long scroll I'd clamp by index too.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The title needs text change by section? → derivedStateOf on layoutInfo mapped to a section key.
  • 120 Hz device? → The problem doubles; same fix.
  • Compose 1.13 computedStateOf? → Docs suggest it for lightweight derivations; verify availability.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a parallax header read scroll offset in composition for two years; moving to graphicsLayer removed a persistent jank report without touching rows.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: wraps in remember or blames rows.
  • Hire: derivedStateOf for the boolean, lambda-based modifier for alpha.
  • Strong hire: explains phases (composition vs layout vs draw reads), validates with Layout Inspector.

questions.contextHtml: A messaging app (800k DAU) is rebuilding the chat screen in Compose. Requirements: newest at bottom, loading older messages when scrolling up (Paging, 30 per page), new incoming messages auto-scroll only if the user is at the bottom, otherwise show a "N new messages" pill, and the position must survive rotation. Prototype with LazyColumn and reverseLayout = false jumps visibly when older pages load (users lose their place) and starts at the top of the list instead of the bottom. A teammate suggests reversing the list data in the ViewModel instead.
questions.promptHtml: What design do you choose, and what are the trade-offs?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Call scrollToItem(lastIndex) whenever the list changes." That fights the user and breaks reading history.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are messages in a local DB (single source of truth)? Do we support jump-to-message (search)? Max loaded window? Do date headers exist? Do edits/deletes happen live?
  2. Immediate mitigation: (Prototype stage) None needed; pick a model.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked / options: (a) reverseLayout = true with data newest-first: index 0 is the newest at the bottom; older messages append at the end, so "prepending" becomes "appending" and the viewport anchors at index 0 naturally. (b) Normal layout with manual scroll compensation on prepend: fragile. (c) Reverse the data in the ViewModel but not the layout: starts at top, still jumps.
  4. How I'd verify each: UI tests: load older page while viewing the middle and assert the first visible key is unchanged; rotation test; insert a message while scrolled up.
  5. Root cause: Default position is index 0 at top; in a normal layout, inserting above shifts content unless anchored by key.
  6. Fix: Choose (a):
LazyColumn(state = listState, reverseLayout = true) {
    items(count = msgs.itemCount, key = msgs.itemKey { it.id }) { i -> msgs[i]?.let { Bubble(it) } }
}
val atBottom by remember { derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex == 0 } }

New message arrives: if atBottom at time of arrival, animateScrollToItem(0); otherwise increment pill count. Data is newest-first from Room (ORDER BY ts DESC), Paging append loads older. Date headers become footers semantically (in reverse layout a header after its group is rendered above it); use stickyHeader after the group in data order and test. 7. Prevention: Tests for the three flows (older page load, new message at bottom, new message while scrolled up). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: (a) costs: "reverse" semantics confuse padding/headers/accessibility order (TalkBack reading order must be verified); not forcing auto-scroll; not reversing data only.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Jump to a search result 5k messages old? → Load a window around the anchor (Paging with initial key) and scrollToItem.
  • Keyboard opens (IME)? → imePadding plus keep bottom anchored; verify behaviour with reverseLayout.
  • Message edited in place? → Stable key keeps position.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a hand-rolled "adjust scroll on prepend" shipped and drifted by one item whenever images loaded late; moving to reverse layout deleted 80 lines.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: forced scrollToItem.
  • Hire: reverseLayout with keys and an at-bottom check.
  • Strong hire: addresses Paging direction, headers, IME, a11y order, and jump-to-message.

questions.contextHtml: A banking-adjacent app (2.5M DAU) has a RecyclerView transaction list with 4 view types, ListAdapter + DiffUtil, sticky date headers by a library, swipe-to-dismiss via ItemTouchHelper, and Paging 3. The team wants Compose for the new design system. Constraints: no big-bang rewrite, P95 scroll frame time must not regress, crash-free rate must stay at or above 99.8%, releases weekly with staged rollout.
questions.promptHtml: How do you migrate the list safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Rewrite the screen in Compose in one PR."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the baseline (P95 frame time, jank%) on low-end devices? Is the data layer already ViewModel+Paging (yes)? What custom behaviors must be preserved (swipe, sticky headers, selection)? Is the screen hosted in Fragment/Activity? Experiments infrastructure?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (planned change); establish the Macrobenchmark baseline on the existing RV first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (risks): (a) perf regression from no baseline profile/R8; (b) behavior parity gaps (swipe, sticky); (c) item state and keys mapping to getItemId; (d) accessibility regressions; (e) memory/GC differences with Paging.
  4. How I'd verify each: Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric on both implementations, same device pool; JankStats in field per variant; TalkBack tests; screenshot tests.
  5. Root cause (of risk): The two engines have different identity and reuse models, so parity has to be proven, not assumed.
  6. Fix (plan): Phase 1: keep the RV, replace item views with ComposeView rows (ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed so recycling doesn't leak or recompose strangely). Phase 2: new screen behind a remote flag with LazyColumn, collectAsLazyPagingItems, itemKey, itemContentType, SwipeToDismissBox, stickyHeader. Ramp 1%, 10%, 50%, 100% while comparing frame time and crash rate. Phase 3: remove the RV path after two stable releases.
  7. Prevention: Keep both variants under the same benchmark in CI until the old one is deleted; ship baseline profiles with the Compose path.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not wrapping an RV in AndroidView inside a LazyColumn; not removing the flag until rolled out; Phase 1 has known overhead of ComposeViews in RV (measure before committing to it).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Compose variant is 5 ms slower on low-end? → Check release/baseline profile first, then keys/contentType/images; hold ramp.
  • ItemTouchHelper drag-reorder? → No built-in Compose equivalent; verify a library or custom gesture, or keep RV for that screen.
  • Mixed Fragments? → ComposeView with the right lifecycle strategy.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: the first Compose variant looked 30% slower until the baseline profile and R8 were enabled for the benchmark app, which flipped the result.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: big-bang rewrite.
  • Hire: flagged, staged, benchmarked migration.
  • Strong hire: phase plan, parity checklist, rollback gates, ComposeView lifecycle handling.

questions.contextHtml:
A classifieds app (1.2M DAU) crashes at 1.1% of sessions on the search results list after a backend change. Stack:

java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Key "88213" was already used. If you are using LazyColumn/Row please make sure you provide a unique key for each item.

The list uses items(count = items.itemCount, key = items.itemKey { it.listingId }). The backend now returns promoted listings that may also appear in organic results on a later page. A prior release was fine; the app version didn't change, only the backend. Red herring: the team suspects an OOM since crashes concentrate on low-RAM devices (long sessions on those devices scroll deeper).
questions.promptHtml: Mitigate, root-cause and make the list robust.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Remove the key." That hides the crash and silently breaks state, animations and scroll anchoring.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can the backend be rolled back or flagged? Is listingId the real identity or is (listingId + slot type)? Do promoted and organic cards render differently? How deep do users page? Is there Room in between?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ask the backend to roll back/dedupe; client hotfix: dedupe in the PagingSource/repository or make keys composite.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) same id on different pages (message says key reuse); (b) concurrent refresh/append duplicates; (c) OOM (red herring, the exception type says otherwise).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log ids on append in a debug build; unit test PagingSource with fixture containing duplicates using TestPager; Crashlytics custom key of the dup id.
  5. Root cause: The server's data model changed so listingId is no longer unique in the combined list. Lazy layouts require unique keys across the whole list, and duplicates throw.
  6. Fix: Short-term: composite key including the placement: key = items.itemKey { "${it.placement}_${it.listingId}" }. Long-term: dedupe organic vs promoted in the repository (promoted wins), and treat the key as part of the API contract with the backend.
  7. Prevention: Contract tests on the paging payload; a runtime guard in debug that asserts uniqueness; alert on IllegalArgumentException key crash signature.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not index keys (state and animation bugs); not try/catch around composition; composite keys change rememberSaveable identity for items already in saved state (acceptable).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Same listing legitimately shown twice? → Then identity must include the placement, as above.
  • Key as Pair? → Not Bundle-saveable; use a String.
  • How would a debug guard work? → Check duplicates in the mapper that builds the UI list.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a crash spike with no app release traced to an A/B ranking test that inserted duplicates; the lesson was to treat server data as untrusted at the list boundary.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: removes key or blames OOM.
  • Hire: composite key or dedupe, rollback request.
  • Strong hire: contract tests, monitoring signature, saveable-key implications.

questions.contextHtml: A streaming app's home screen: LazyColumn of rails, each a LazyRow of posters. Today: 8 rails with 20 items. Product wants personalised homes with 60 rails × 50 items, with rails loaded lazily from the network, on devices ranging from 3 GB RAM phones to Android TV. Currently: P95 frame time 21 ms, memory 310 MB on a 3 GB device, and the Perfetto trace shows ~12 ms composition per rail when it first appears. Back navigation resets each rail's scroll position to the start.
questions.promptHtml: What breaks at 10x and how do you redesign?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Load everything and rely on laziness."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are rails fetched in one payload or per rail? Poster image sizes? Android TV focus requirements? Do we need rail state restored? What's the memory budget per device class?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap items per rail loaded initially (e.g. 12), size-limit images, fix back-navigation state.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) images decoded at full size per poster: dominant memory; (b) unbounded items lists per rail kept in the ViewModel state; (c) first-appearance composition cost (12 ms): not prefetched; (d) per-row state not saved so scroll resets.
